name: GAN - Lecturer A: Implementation & Code
voiceSnippet: Today we are implementing GANs in PyTorch. Focus on the training loop code. Notice how we compute the BCE loss separately for the discriminator on real labels and fake labels, and then zero the generator gradients before calling backward.
documentSnippet: Section 4: PyTorch GAN Implementation. Generator class, Discriminator class, Adam optimizer configurations, BCEWithLogitsLoss.

name: GAN - Lecturer B: Conceptual Dynamics & Exploration
voiceSnippet: Don't worry about coding or PyTorch today; we want to explore the conceptual game between the generator and discriminator. Think of it as a counterfeiter and a detective. Explore what happens if the discriminator gets too good too fast—if the detective catches everything immediately, what feedback does the counterfeiter actually receive?
documentSnippet: Adversarial Training Dynamics. Minimax objective, zero-sum game, discriminator loss saturation.

name: Concurrency - Lecturer A: SQL Syntax & Lock Primitives
voiceSnippet: Look at the SQL script on slide 3. We issue SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on table accounts. Pay attention to the syntax and lock flags. Practice writing the exact lock acquisition query.
documentSnippet: SQL syntax: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE [NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED]. Row-level exclusive lock syntax.

name: Concurrency - Lecturer B: ACID Anomalies & Trade-off Philosophy
voiceSnippet: Forget about SQL syntax today. We are exploring the philosophical trade-off between performance and anomalies. What happens if a banking system allows non-repeatable reads? Why did the database architects decide that Read Committed should tolerate phantom rows? Think about the trade-off.
documentSnippet: ANSI SQL Isolation Levels. Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read anomaly taxonomy.

name: Consensus - Lecturer A: Packet Tracing & Wire Formats
voiceSnippet: Trace the exact RequestVote RPC packet. Bytes 0 to 3 are term number, bytes 4 to 7 are candidate ID. Follow the wire trace when a network packet drops.
documentSnippet: Raft RPC wire protocol specifications. RequestVote arguments and return values.

name: Consensus - Lecturer B: Split-Brain & Quorum Dynamics
voiceSnippet: Don't memorize packet formats. Explore what happens during a network partition. If three nodes are in London and two in New York, what happens if both sides attempt to elect a leader? Why can the majority continue while the minority must pause?
documentSnippet: Quorum intersection property: any two majorities of size (N/2)+1 must share at least one node.

name: Negative Boundary: Explicit No Coding (FFT Butterfly)
voiceSnippet: We will study the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm, but I want to make one thing completely clear: do not write Python code, do not worry about NumPy implementations, and there will be zero coding questions on this exam. We only care about the divide-and-conquer butterfly concept.
documentSnippet: FFT algorithm: Cooley-Tukey butterfly operations, O(N log N) recurrence relation.

name: Negative Boundary: Explicit No Math Derivations (Master Theorem)
voiceSnippet: The textbook gives a 5-page mathematical proof deriving the regularity condition of Master Theorem Case 3. Skip that proof entirely! I will not ask you to derive a*f(n/b) <= c*f(n). You only need to recognize which case matches the recurrence.
documentSnippet: Theorem 4.1 Master Theorem Case 3 Proof with regularity condition derivation.

name: Negative Boundary: Strict Subsystem Scope (CPU Decode Stage)
voiceSnippet: Today we are looking strictly at CPU instruction decode stages. We are not covering memory caching, we are not covering branch prediction, and we are not covering out-of-order execution today. Keep your attention strictly on 5-stage classic RISC decode.
documentSnippet: Pipelined Processors: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback.

name: Negative Boundary: No Vendor-Specific Tools (Linux cgroups)
voiceSnippet: In this container security overview, don't worry about specific Docker CLI flags or AWS ECS configurations. Focus purely on Linux kernel cgroups and namespaces as isolation mechanisms.
documentSnippet: Container isolation: cgroups v2 resource limits, pid/net namespaces.

name: Conceptual-Hard Feasibility: CAP Theorem Trade-off Dynamics
voiceSnippet: In distributed storage, you cannot have both linearizable consistency and 100% availability during network partitions. Think about why: if a network cable is cut between two datacenters, you must make a fundamental philosophical choice: do you reject incoming writes to keep data consistent, or accept writes and allow data to diverge?
documentSnippet: Brewer's CAP Theorem: In the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability.

name: Conceptual-Hard Feasibility: Microservices vs Monolith Trade-offs
voiceSnippet: Microservices are not a silver bullet. You trade operational simplicity for team autonomy. With a monolith, you have one deployment artifact and zero distributed transaction issues, but teams step on each other's toes. With microservices, teams deploy independently, but you introduce eventual consistency, network latency, and distributed tracing nightmares.
documentSnippet: Software Architecture Styles: Monolithic vs Service-Oriented vs Microservices.

name: Conceptual-Hard Feasibility: Zero-Knowledge Proofs Intuition
voiceSnippet: Imagine the Ali Baba cave with a secret door. How can Peggy prove to Victor that she knows the secret passphrase without revealing the passphrase to Victor? Observe how repeated trials of choosing paths reduce Victor's doubt exponentially.
documentSnippet: Zero-Knowledge Interactive Proofs: Completeness, Soundness, Zero-Knowledge properties.

name: Conceptual-Hard Feasibility: Public Key Cryptography Trust Models
voiceSnippet: Why do we need Certificate Authorities? If Alice sends her public key over an untrusted network, Bob has no way of knowing whether the key belongs to Alice or to Mallory performing a man-in-the-middle attack. Explore why encryption without authentication is meaningless.
documentSnippet: Public Key Infrastructure: Digital Certificates, X.509, Root CAs, Man-in-the-Middle attack.

name: True Deficit: Cloud Service Catalog Overview
voiceSnippet: Welcome to Cloud 101. Amazon EC2 stands for Elastic Compute Cloud; it gives you virtual servers. S3 stands for Simple Storage Service; it stores files as objects. IAM stands for Identity and Access Management; it manages users and passwords.
documentSnippet: AWS Services Overview: EC2, S3, IAM, RDS.

name: True Deficit: Physical Network Media Overview
voiceSnippet: Network cables come in three common types: twisted pair copper cables like Cat 6, coaxial cables with copper shielding, and fiber optic cables made of glass strands that transmit pulses of light.
documentSnippet: Physical Layer Media: UTP, STP, Coaxial, Single-mode and Multi-mode Fiber.

name: True Deficit: Software Engineering Roles Definitions
voiceSnippet: In modern tech companies, Product Managers define what to build, UX Designers create the wireframes and user journeys, Software Engineers write the software, and QA Engineers test for bugs.
documentSnippet: Agile Development Team Roles and Responsibilities.

name: Intent Marker: Explore what happens if...
voiceSnippet: Explore what happens if we double the batch size during stochastic gradient descent. Does the training trajectory become smoother, and what happens to the generalization gap on test data?
documentSnippet: Stochastic Gradient Descent: Batch size dynamics, generalization error.

name: Intent Marker: Why does this happen?
voiceSnippet: Why does a 2-phase locking protocol prevent cascading aborts in Strict 2PL, whereas standard 2PL permits them? Think carefully about the exact point where exclusive locks are released.
documentSnippet: Strict Two-Phase Locking (S2PL) vs Standard 2PL. Cascading rollbacks.

name: Intent Marker: Compare the difference...
voiceSnippet: Compare the difference between optimistic concurrency control and pessimistic locking. When the collision probability is under 1%, which one yields higher system throughput?
documentSnippet: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) vs Pessimistic 2PL.

name: Intent Marker: Follow each step / Trace
voiceSnippet: Follow each step as a packet travels through a NAT router. First it modifies the source IP, then it writes to the translation table, then it recomputes the checksum.
documentSnippet: Network Address Translation: Port mapping, IP rewrite sequence.

name: Intent Marker: Focus on writing / coding
voiceSnippet: Focus on writing the recursive helper function. Make sure your base case checks for null pointers before you access left and right children.
documentSnippet: Binary Tree Traversal: Recursive implementation, null pointer base cases.
